What adverse possession means

Adverse possession lets a person claim ownership of land they have openly used, against the true owner's wishes, for long enough. It is a doctrine that allows someone to gain a property right in land owned by another, and people sometimes call it squatters' rights.

The plain definition is enjoyment of real property with a claim of right, opposed to another person's claim, that is continuous, exclusive, hostile, open and notorious. The idea is to reward productive use of land and to punish owners who sleep on their rights.

Typical examples are steady use of a private road or driveway and farming an unused parcel. Those look very different from a stranger walking into a vacant house, a difference the rest of this guide returns to.

How long a claimant must possess the land

Twenty years. Under G.L. c. 260, section 21, an action to recover land must be brought within twenty years after the right of action or entry first accrued, or within twenty years after the claimant or those they claim under were seized or possessed of the premises.

Related sections matter too. Section 22 deals with time spent by a predecessor, which counts toward the period, and section 28 deals with open possession. If you inherited a house, ask what happened on the land in earlier owners' time, not only during your own.

The Appeals Court case 1148 Davol Street LLC v. Mechanic's Mill One LLC, 86 Mass. App. Ct. 748 (2014), added that a claim against a private party can begin to accrue while the land was still publicly owned. Time can run in the background longer than owners expect.

Section 21 itself contains one exception: it does not bar an action by or on behalf of a nonprofit land conservation corporation or trust for land held for conservation, parks, recreation, water protection or wildlife protection.

What a squatter has to prove

The claimant carries the burden and must prove every element. Holmes v. Johnson, 324 Mass. 450 (1949), says the burden of proof extends to all the necessary elements of such possession.

Older and newer cases word the elements in similar ways. Cook v. Babcock (1853) calls for actual, open, exclusive and adverse possession and says failure to establish any one is fatal. Ryan v. Stavros, 348 Mass. 251 (1964), puts it as nonpermissive use that is actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse for twenty years.

  • Open and notorious: visible enough that a reasonable owner would notice.
  • Exclusive: not shared with the owner or the public.
  • Hostile or nonpermissive: without the owner's permission. Use you allowed in writing or by word is a weak foundation for a claim.
  • Continuous for the full period.

Miller v. Abramson, 95 Mass. App. Ct. 828 (2019), shows that ordinary care can be enough. In that suburban dispute over a sliver of land, mowing and maintaining it as an average owner would supported a finding of adverse possession.

Land that cannot be taken by adverse possession

Registered land, land held by the Commonwealth, and railroad property cannot be taken this way. Three statutes say so.

Land typeStatute
Registered land (Land Court Certificate of Title)G.L. c. 185, section 53
Land held by the CommonwealthG.L. c. 7C, section 32
Railroad propertyG.L. c. 160, section 88

Owners most often benefit from the registered land rule. Section 53 of chapter 185 says no title to registered land, or easement or other right in it against the registered owner, may be gained by prescription or adverse possession, and no right of way by necessity is implied in a conveyance of registered land. If your deed history shows a Certificate of Title, that protection applies.

Whether your parcel is registered or recorded is a title question your attorney or the registry can answer in a few minutes.

Is a squatter the same as an adverse possessor?

No. A person who walks into a vacant house is a trespasser, not someone building a twenty year claim. Adverse possession is not the same as trespassing, and trespass has its own statute.

That statute is G.L. c. 266, section 120. It punishes someone who, without right, enters or remains in a dwelling house, building or improved or enclosed land of another after being forbidden by the person with lawful control, whether directly or by posted notice. The penalty is a fine of up to $100, or up to thirty days in jail, or both. A police officer, sheriff, deputy sheriff or constable may arrest a person found trespassing and hold them up to twenty four hours, Sunday excepted, until a complaint can be made.

The statute has a significant limit. It does not apply to tenants or occupants of residential premises who rightfully entered at the start of a tenancy or occupancy and stay after it has ended or is alleged to have ended. For those people the owner or landlord may recover possession only through appropriate civil proceedings.

What to do about an unauthorized occupant

Document the situation, give a clear written notice that the person is not allowed to stay, and get advice before acting yourself. The right route depends on how the person got in, which is exactly the line section 120 draws between trespassers and people who entered with permission.

  • Someone who never had permission: forbid entry in writing or by posted notice, then involve the police under the trespass statute.
  • Someone who entered as a tenant or occupant and stayed: do not change locks or remove belongings. The statute says possession may be recovered only through civil proceedings.
  • A boundary or use dispute with a neighbor: that is a title question, and a quiet title action in the Land Court is one way owners address it.

Keep dated photographs, copies of any lease or message exchange, and utility records. They show who was in the house and under what terms, and a buyer's attorney will ask for them.

How an occupant claim affects selling

An open dispute over who has the right to occupy or own the land complicates a conventional sale, because a buyer's lender and title attorney need clear title and, usually, possession at closing. That is general closing practice rather than a statute, and your own attorney should confirm what applies to your property.

Deeds to recorded land are filed with the registry of deeds, and under G.L. c. 183, section 4, a conveyance is not valid against most third parties unless recorded. A claim based on long possession is a question about facts on the ground, so ask your attorney how it would show up in a title review.

If you own a house with an unresolved occupant, you can describe the situation to Cash Home Buyers and see whether an as-is purchase fits. An attorney should look at the legal side before any papers are signed.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter take ownership of my Massachusetts house?

Only by meeting every element for the full twenty years. G.L. c. 260, section 21 sets the period, and the claimant must prove actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse possession without permission. A short stay does not qualify.

How many years does adverse possession take in Massachusetts?

Twenty years under G.L. c. 260, section 21. Time spent by a predecessor in possession can count toward that period under section 22.

Can adverse possession happen on registered land?

No. G.L. c. 185, section 53 says no title to registered land can be acquired by prescription or adverse possession.

Can I remove a squatter myself?

If the person is a trespasser who never had permission, the police can act under G.L. c. 266, section 120. If the person entered as a tenant or occupant, the same section says possession can be recovered only through civil proceedings, so do not use self help.

Is trespassing a crime in Massachusetts?

Yes. Section 120 sets a fine up to $100, up to thirty days in jail, or both, once a person is forbidden to be on the property and stays or returns.

Lease or tenancy at will?

Massachusetts recognizes two main kinds of tenancy: a lease for a fixed term and a tenancy at will. The rights of landlord and tenant depend partly on which one exists, so if you are thinking about selling a rented house, the first job is to work out which one your renter actually has.

With a lease, the rent stays the same for the term, usually one year, and the landlord cannot end the tenancy unless the tenant fails to meet the lease conditions. A tenancy at will lasts until either side properly ends it. Many people call it month-to-month, and sometimes there is no written agreement at all.

Where rent is paid monthly, either side ends an at-will tenancy by giving notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer. Rent can change on the same notice. A tenant who pays weekly is also at will, and the termination notice rule stays the same.

What a landlord can collect at the start

A landlord may ask for only four things up front: first month's rent, a security deposit, last month's rent, and the actual cost of a new lock and key. The deposit cannot be more than one month's rent.

Up-front itemRule
First month's rentAllowed
Security depositCovers damage beyond normal wear and tear, capped at one month's rent
Last month's rentAllowed, with a signed receipt
Lock and keyOnly the actual cost of a new lock and key
Pet, broker or application feesNot allowed at the start of a tenancy

A law that took effect on August 1, 2025 also bars brokers and salespeople from charging tenants fees when they mainly serve the landlord, and a landlord still cannot pass on a fee for a broker's work for the landlord.

Handling the security deposit

The deposit goes into an interest-bearing account at a Massachusetts bank within the first month of the tenancy, kept apart from the landlord's own money. The tenant is entitled to the bank's name and address and the account number.

  • Each year the landlord either pays the interest to the tenant or lets the tenant deduct it from rent.
  • A statement of condition is due within 10 days of the tenancy start or of receiving the deposit, whichever is later, and the tenant then has 15 days to add to it.
  • At move-out the deposit plus interest comes back within 30 days.
  • If the landlord keeps part of it for damage, a written description and a repair estimate are due within 30 days of move-out.

If you plan to sell a rented house, these records will come up. Gather the receipts, the bank details and the statement of condition before you talk to any buyer.

Can a landlord show a rented house to buyers?

Yes, but only by arrangement. The landlord must set up a time with the tenant in advance to enter the unit to make repairs, inspect it, or show it to prospective tenants, buyers or real estate agents.

Entry without approval is limited to two situations: a mechanical or repair emergency with the potential to damage the whole building, or an apparent abandonment of the apartment. A planned showing for a buyer is neither. If you sell with a tenant in place, expect to schedule every visit around the renter.

Some owners of occupied rentals prefer a buyer who will purchase as-is without repeated walk-throughs. Whichever route you take, keep communication with the tenant calm and in writing.

Repair duties while the house is for sale

The landlord must keep the unit habitable for the whole tenancy, and listing the house for sale does not change that. The State Sanitary Code, 105 CMR 410, sets the minimum standards, and the right to habitable housing covers every occupant, not only the named tenant.

If a landlord does not respond, a tenant can ask a code enforcement officer or the local board of health to inspect, and an inspector can order the landlord to fix violations. A tenant who cannot get repairs may in some cases withhold part of the rent or move out, and should talk to a lawyer or legal services first.

Lead paint adds another layer. For a rental built before 1978, landlord and tenant must sign and keep the Tenant Lead Law Notification and Tenant Certification. If a child under six will live there, the landlord must delead or bring the hazards under interim control, and cannot refuse to rent to a family with young children because of lead.

Retaliation

Retaliation is any threat or reprisal against a tenant or occupant for using a legal right. A rushed sale plan can look like retaliation if it follows a tenant's complaint, so watch the timing.

Protected activity includes reporting conditions to the landlord or the board of health, filing a complaint in court or with an agency, and joining a tenants' union. Illegal reprisals include:

  • Raising the rent or refusing to renew a lease.
  • Changing the locks or shutting off heat or electricity.
  • Starting an eviction.
  • Reporting a tenant to the police or to immigration officials.
  • Harassing a tenant or other occupant.

Certain landlord conduct within six months of a tenant's protected activity is presumed retaliatory. In a lawsuit, a court would assume the action was a reprisal unless the landlord proves otherwise.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Massachusetts houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Illegal lease terms

A lease cannot contain several terms that landlords sometimes copy from old forms. These are illegal:

  • Making the tenant pay to repair ordinary wear and tear.
  • Requiring professional cleaning at the end of the lease.
  • Making the tenant pay for repairs to parts of the building outside the apartment.
  • Barring the tenant from suing the landlord or reporting Sanitary Code violations.
  • Barring the tenant from joining a tenants' union.
  • Charging a late fee when rent is less than 30 days late.

A lease must also name the owner, the person responsible for maintenance, and the person who accepts formal notices, with addresses and phone numbers. If the landlord holds a deposit, the lease must show the amount and explain the tenant's rights to it. Check your own lease against this list before you share it with anyone.

How eviction works if you need the house empty

A Massachusetts landlord cannot remove a tenant without a court's permission. Physically removing the tenant or their belongings, or changing the locks, is not allowed.

The usual path starts with a notice, most often a Notice to Quit, whose length depends on the tenancy type and the reason. The landlord then files a Summary Process case, which begins when the tenant is served a Summons and Complaint. The tenant can raise defenses such as improper termination, uncorrected known problems, retaliation, or discrimination, including a failure to grant a reasonable accommodation.

If the landlord wins, the court issues a judgment and then an execution, which lets a sheriff or constable carry out a physical eviction. The tenant's property goes to an approved public warehouse, the landlord pays the moving fees and is entitled to reimbursement, and the tenant gets one opportunity to claim items of personal or sentimental value. Because the process takes time, owners who need to sell quickly often weigh it against a sale to a buyer who accepts the tenant in place.

Fire department certificate for one and two family homes

A seller needs a certificate of compliance showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the rules for a sale or transfer. Call the local fire department as soon as you have a closing date.

The requirements depend on when the home was built and when the last building permit was issued. Battery-powered smoke alarms more than 10 years old, or expired, must be replaced with 10-year sealed units that are photoelectric and have a hush feature. An alarm with no manufacture date counts as expired. The fire department charges a fee, so ask the local office what it is.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Before you sell a tenant-occupied house

Start by confirming the tenancy type and any lease end date, then gather the deposit records and any repair complaints. How an existing lease or at-will tenancy is treated when the property changes hands is a question for a Massachusetts real estate attorney, so ask before you sign anything.

The Attorney General's Consumer Hotline at (617) 727-8400 answers general questions about landlord and tenant rules, and a local board of health can explain Sanitary Code issues. When you are ready to talk about a sale, bring the lease, rent ledger, deposit receipts and any inspection notices.

Frequently asked questions

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Massachusetts?

Either side must give notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer. The same timing applies to a rent change.

Can a Massachusetts landlord keep a security deposit for normal wear and tear?

No. A landlord may keep unpaid rent and the cost of damage beyond normal wear and tear, and must return the rest with interest within 30 days. A lease may not make the tenant pay for ordinary wear.

Can I enter a rented house to show it to a buyer without asking?

No. The landlord must arrange the visit with the tenant in advance. Entry without approval is allowed only for an emergency that could damage the whole building or an apparent abandonment.

Do I need court approval to evict a tenant before I sell?

Yes. A landlord cannot evict by removing the tenant, removing belongings or changing locks. The landlord gives proper notice, files a summary process case, and only a sheriff or constable carries out a physical eviction after a judgment and execution.

What do I need from the fire department to sell a one or two family home?

A certificate of compliance showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the requirements for a sale or transfer. Call the local fire department when you have a closing date and ask about its fee.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Massachusetts?
We buy Massachusetts houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Notice to quit: the first step

Before any eviction case can start, a Massachusetts landlord has to end the tenancy with a written notice to quit. Getting one does not mean the tenant must leave right away. Only a court order can force a move.

How many days the notice gives depends on the reason and on the kind of tenancy. Below you will find each version, how a notice has to be delivered, and what changes if you own the house and plan to sell it.

How many days does each notice give?

Fourteen days applies to unpaid rent. Thirty days is the usual figure for most other reasons.

SituationWritten notice
Rent not paid14 days, unless the lease says otherwise
Rent not paid, federally assisted housingA 30-day notice may be used
Month-to-month tenancy at willAt least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental period
Lease violation, or landlord wants the unit back30 days
Lease that has run outNo notice needed, since the lease sets the end date

The statute for a tenancy at will is worded a bit differently from that plain summary. It speaks of three months' notice, and when rent is paid at shorter intervals, the notice must equal the gap between payment days or thirty days, whichever is longer. If rent dates sit further apart than thirty days, the notice can stretch accordingly.

Can a tenant stop a 14-day notice by paying?

Sometimes. Under G.L. c. 186, section 12, a tenant who has not received a similar notice in the previous twelve months keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering the full rent due within ten days after receiving the notice.

Every nonpayment notice must carry a short statement about this right. If it is missing, the tenant's time to pay runs to the day the answer is due in a court case, though the omission does not otherwise ruin the notice. When a late payment traces back to a delay by a federal, state or municipal agency, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and can treat the tenancy as never terminated if everything owed is tendered.

Paying arrears by an agreed date is called curing the problem. Other points that come up in nonpayment cases:

  • The RAFT program offers emergency payments of up to $7,000 per year to eligible households behind on rent.
  • A tenant with a pending RAFT application cannot be evicted, and should tell the court about it.
  • The landlord must attach a form listing rental assistance programs to a nonpayment notice.
  • A payment plan worked out with the landlord can also stop the case from moving forward.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Massachusetts house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a valid notice must contain

A valid notice names the exact day the tenancy ends and, for most reasons, says why the landlord is ending it. The notice exists to end the tenancy, so the tenant has to actually receive it for it to work.

  • A written notice, except where a lease simply expires.
  • The specific date on which the tenancy will end.
  • The reason, when the cause is a lease violation or unpaid rent.
  • The statutory right-to-pay statement, for nonpayment.
  • The rental assistance form, for nonpayment.

No single delivery method is required. A landlord can hand the notice to the tenant, ideally with a disinterested person present. Two common shortcuts fail: a constable leaving the notice at the tenant's last usual address when the tenant never actually receives it, and a mailed notice the tenant does not pick up. Sample forms are available through the Trial Court Law Libraries, with a warning that they may not be legally sufficient in every case.

Why the calendar matters, especially around February

A month-to-month notice has to expire at the end of a rental period, so the date it is served decides when the tenancy can end. One example from the Court System: a notice served too late in January cannot end the tenancy by March 1, because February is shorter than thirty days.

An older notice does not always have to be repeated. A landlord who served one months ago generally does not need a new one, unless the right to evict was waived. That can happen by accepting rent in advance without a written reservation of rights, or by signing a new rental agreement that created a fresh tenancy. If you have taken a late rent payment since serving notice, ask an attorney whether the notice still stands.

What a landlord cannot do while the notice runs

A landlord cannot lock the tenant out, shut off services or use force to regain the home. Both the state's tenant guide and the statute say only a judge's order can remove a tenant.

Under G.L. c. 186, section 14, a landlord who willfully fails to supply water, heat, light, power or gas, interferes with quiet enjoyment, or tries to regain possession by force without judicial process faces a fine of $25 to $300 or up to six months in jail. The tenant can also recover actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

Evicting for an illegal reason is also off limits. Examples include a tenant reporting violations to health inspectors or withholding rent because of bad conditions.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Massachusetts houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does selling the house change the notice?

Selling does not shorten anything. A no-fault notice to quit can be used because the landlord wants to sell, but it still means the landlord plans to take the tenant to court, and the case still appears on the tenant's housing record.

A sale also carries duties that follow the tenancy. Under section 15B of the same chapter:

  • A landlord who transfers the building, by sale or otherwise, must pass the security deposit and its accrued interest to the new owner.
  • The new owner must tell the tenant in writing within forty-five days that the deposit was transferred.
  • If the old owner fails to transfer it, the new owner becomes liable for the deposit anyway.
  • Rent paid in advance for the last month must likewise be credited to the buyer, who must give notice within forty-five days.
  • A lease can allow the landlord to enter to show the home to a prospective purchaser.

Massachusetts expects a tenancy to continue across a sale unless it is properly ended. Before listing a rented house, ask a real estate attorney how the lease or tenancy at will carries over.

Problems owners of rented houses run into

Most trouble comes from a notice that is late, incomplete or served in a way the tenant never actually received. A notice the tenant never received is not adequate notice, and that hurts most when a closing date is already set.

  • Special rules apply to mobile home parks, rooming houses, dormitories, residential superintendents and public housing.
  • Government-subsidized rent may require the notice to state specific reasons, so check both the lease and the program rules.
  • The step after an expired notice is a summary process summons and complaint, which a constable or sheriff must serve.
  • Free mediation is available through the Community Mediation Centers, and most courts offer it as well.

Some owners sell with the tenant still living in the house. Others settle on a move-out date by agreement, which can work when a landlord offers a little extra time. Either route should be written down and reviewed by a lawyer. A cash sale to a buyer who accepts the house with the tenant in it skips the wait for a vacant unit, though the deposit and rent transfers described above still apply.

Frequently asked questions

How many days is a Massachusetts eviction notice?

It is 14 days for unpaid rent and 30 days for most other reasons. A month-to-month tenancy at will needs at least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental period, and the statute can call for more when rent dates are further apart.

Does a notice to quit mean the tenant has to leave?

No. A notice to quit is only the first step. The tenant can stay until a court orders otherwise, and a landlord cannot change the locks or remove belongings before then.

Can a landlord send a notice because the house is being sold?

Yes. That is a no-fault notice to quit. It still leads to a court case if the tenant does not leave, and the sale does not cancel the tenant's rights in the meantime.

Does the notice have to be mailed or hand delivered?

No single method is required, but the tenant must actually receive it. A notice left at an old address, or mailed and never picked up, is not adequate notice.

What happens to the security deposit when a rented house is sold?

The seller must transfer the deposit and accrued interest to the buyer, and the buyer must notify the tenant in writing within forty-five days. A buyer remains liable for the deposit even if the seller fails to transfer it.
